question: List three operations that convert an analog signal into a PCM bit stream.
answer:
• Sampling selects values at chosen times.

  • Quantization replaces each value with an allowed amplitude level.

  • Encoding assigns bits to each level.

question: Sketch a continuous sinusoid and its uniformly spaced samples. Label the axes and sampling interval.
answer:
The smooth curve is the analog signal. Each stem ends at the measured value at \(t=nT_s\). Adjacent stems are separated by \(T_s\); their heights need not be equal.

Horizontal axis: time. Vertical axis: voltage. The curve is continuous; stems mark measured samples. The uniform horizontal spacing is the sampling interval.

question: Explain why sampling alone does not produce binary data.
answer: Sampling makes time discrete, but the sample amplitude can still take any real value. Quantization and binary encoding are required to obtain a finite binary representation.

question: Why is an anti-aliasing filter placed before the sampler?
answer: It attenuates input components above the intended sampling band. Otherwise, these components can fold into the useful band, where a later filter cannot separate them from the desired signal.

question: If adjacent sampled-spectrum replicas overlap, what is this effect called, and how can it be avoided?
answer: The overlap indicates aliasing. Increase the sampling rate, reduce the input bandwidth before sampling, or do both. For a baseband signal, use \(f_s>2B\) with a practical transition margin.

question: For \(x(t)=3\cos(1200\pi t+\pi/3)\) V, with \(t\) in seconds, find peak amplitude, frequency, period and \(x(0)\).
answer:
Sinusoidal signal parameters\[\begin{aligned} x(t)=A\cos(\omega t+\phi)\\[2pt]f=\omega/(2\pi)\\[2pt]T=1/f \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Compare with the standard cosine.\[\begin{aligned} x(t)=A\cos(2\pi ft+\phi)\\[2pt]A=3\text{ V}\\[2pt]\phi=\pi/3 \end{aligned}\]

Convert angular frequency to hertz.\[\begin{aligned} f&=\frac{1200\pi}{2\pi}\\[2pt]&=600\text{ Hz} \end{aligned}\]

Take the reciprocal and evaluate the initial phase.\[\begin{aligned} T&=\frac1{600}\\[2pt]&=1.667\text{ ms}\\[2pt]x(0)&=3\cos(\pi/3)\\[2pt]&=1.5\text{ V} \end{aligned}\]

\(A=3\) V; \(f=600\) Hz; \(T=1.667\) ms; \(x(0)=1.5\) V.

question: A sampler operates at \(f_s=8\) ksample/s. Find \(T_s\) and the time of sample \(n=6\), starting with \(n=0\) at \(t=0\).
answer:
Sampling interval and sampling instants\[\begin{aligned} T_s=1/f_s\\[2pt]t_n=nT_s \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Take the reciprocal.\[\begin{aligned} T_s&=\frac1{8000}\\[2pt]&=125\,\mu\text{s} \end{aligned}\]

Multiply by the index.\[\begin{aligned} t_6&=6T_s\\[2pt]&=6(125)\\[2pt]&=750\,\mu\text{s} \end{aligned}\]

\(T_s=125\,\mu\)s and \(t_6=0.75\) ms.

question: Sample \(x(t)=2\cos(2\pi1000t)\) V at 4 ksample/s. Find \(x[n]\) and its first five values.
answer:
Discrete-time sampling relation\[\begin{aligned} x[n]=x(nT_s)\\[2pt]T_s=1/f_s \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Replace time by the sample instant.\[\begin{aligned} x[n]&=2\cos(2\pi1000n/4000)\\[2pt]&=2\cos(\pi n/2) \end{aligned}\]

Evaluate at integer indices.\[(x[0],x[1],x[2],x[3],x[4])=(2,0,-2,0,2)\text{ V}\]

\(x[n]=2\cos(\pi n/2)\) V; the sequence repeats every four samples.

question: A uniform midpoint 3-bit quantizer covers \([-1,+1)\) V. Find the number of levels, step and maximum in-range error.
answer:
Uniform quantizer resolution\[\begin{aligned} L=2^b\\[2pt]\Delta=(V_{\max}-V_{\min})/L\\[2pt]|e_q|_{\max}=\Delta/2 \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Count codewords.\[\begin{aligned} L&=2^3\\[2pt]&=8 \end{aligned}\]

Divide the full range into equal bins.\[\begin{aligned} \Delta&=\frac{1-(-1)}8\\[2pt]&=0.25\text{ V} \end{aligned}\]

Midpoint rounding has a half-bin error bound.\[\begin{aligned} |e_q|\le\Delta/2&=0.25/2\\[2pt]&=0.125\text{ V} \end{aligned}\]

8 levels; \(\Delta=0.25\) V; \(|e_q|\le0.125\) V without overload.

question: An ADC uses 8 bits/sample at 8 ksample/s. Added overhead is 25 percent of payload. Find payload rate, total rate and transmitted bit interval.
answer:
Payload rate and transmission overhead\[\begin{aligned} R_{\rm payload}=bf_s\\[2pt]R_{\rm total}=(1+\alpha)R_{\rm payload}\\[2pt]T_b=1/R_{\rm total} \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Multiply sample rate by word length.\[\begin{aligned} R_{\rm payload}&=8000(8)\\[2pt]&=64000\text{ bit/s} \end{aligned}\]

Add the stated payload-based overhead.\[\begin{aligned} R_{\rm total}&=1.25(64000)\\[2pt]&=80000\text{ bit/s} \end{aligned}\]

Use total transmitted rate for the bit interval.\[\begin{aligned} T_b&=1/80000\\[2pt]&=12.5\,\mu\text{s} \end{aligned}\]

Payload 64 kbit/s; total 80 kbit/s; bit interval 12.5 microseconds.

question: A 10 mW signal experiences 20 dB power loss. Receiver noise power is 0.01 mW. Find received signal power and SNR in linear units and dB.
answer:
Received power and signal-to-noise ratio\[\begin{aligned} P_r=P_t10^{-L_{\rm dB}/10}\\[2pt]\mathrm{SNR}=P_r/P_n \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Convert power loss to a ratio.\[\begin{aligned} P_r&=P_t10^{-20/10}\\[2pt]&=10(0.01)\\[2pt]&=0.1\text{ mW} \end{aligned}\]

Divide signal by noise power.\[\begin{aligned} \mathrm{SNR}&=0.1/0.01\\[2pt]&=10 \end{aligned}\]

Convert the power ratio to decibels.\[\begin{aligned} \mathrm{SNR}_{\rm dB}&=10\log_{10}10\\[2pt]&=10\text{ dB} \end{aligned}\]

\(P_r=0.1\) mW. The linear SNR is 10, corresponding to 10 dB.

question: Use \(+1\) V for bit 1 and \(-1\) V for bit 0, with threshold zero. Decide the received values \(0.8,-0.2,0.1,-1.2\) V. Can the decisions alone prove that no errors occurred?
answer:
Binary threshold decision\[\widehat b=\begin{cases}1,&r\ge0,\\0,&r<0.\end{cases}\]

Substitution / calculation

Apply the threshold separately to each value.

Nonnegative values select 1; negative values select 0.\[\widehat{\mathbf b}=(1,0,1,0)\]

To count errors, compare with the transmitted bits; their values were not supplied.

Decisions 1010; the actual error count cannot be established.

question: Find the Nyquist rate and Nyquist interval for \(x(t)=4\sin(6000\pi t)\).
answer:
Nyquist sampling rate\[\begin{aligned} f_m=\omega/(2\pi)\\[2pt]R_N=2f_m\\[2pt]T_N=1/R_N \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Extract frequency in hertz.\[\begin{aligned} f_m&=6000\pi/(2\pi)\\[2pt]&=3000\text{ Hz} \end{aligned}\]

Double the largest frequency.\[\begin{aligned} R_N&=2f_m\\[2pt]&=2(3000)\\[2pt]&=6000\text{ sample/s} \end{aligned}\]

Find the reciprocal boundary interval.\[\begin{aligned} T_N&=1/6000\\[2pt]&=166.667\,\mu\text{s} \end{aligned}\]

Nyquist rate 6 ksample/s; interval 166.667 microseconds. Use practical margin.

question: Find the spectral frequencies and Nyquist rate of \(x(t)=\cos(2\pi1000t)\cos(2\pi1500t)\).
answer:
Product-to-sum identity and Nyquist rate\[\begin{aligned} \cos a\cos b=\tfrac12\cos(a-b)+\tfrac12\cos(a+b)\\[2pt]R_N=2f_{\max} \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Expand the product.\[\cos a\cos b=\tfrac12\cos(a-b)+\tfrac12\cos(a+b)\]

Identify the difference and sum components.\[x(t)=\tfrac12\cos(2\pi500t)+\tfrac12\cos(2\pi2500t)\]

Double the upper frequency.\[\begin{aligned} R_N&=2(2500)\\[2pt]&=5000\text{ sample/s} \end{aligned}\]

Components at 500 and 2500 Hz; Nyquist rate 5 ksample/s.

question: Sample \(x(t)=8\cos(200\pi t)\) at 150 sample/s. Write the sample sequence and identify its baseband alias.
answer:
Discrete-time frequency periodicity\[\begin{aligned} x[n]=x(n/f_s)\\[2pt]\cos(\theta+2\pi kn)=\cos\theta\\[2pt](k,n\in\mathbb Z) \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Substitute the sample time.\[\begin{aligned} x[n]&=8\cos(200\pi n/150)\\[2pt]&=8\cos(4\pi n/3) \end{aligned}\]

Subtract an integer multiple of 2 pi for integer n.\[\begin{aligned} x[n]&=8\cos(-2\pi n/3)\\[2pt]&=8\cos(2\pi n/3) \end{aligned}\]

Identify the equivalent frequency.\[2\pi f_a/150=2\pi/3\quad\Rightarrow\quad f_a=50\text{ Hz}\]

The samples also represent a 50 Hz cosine.

question: A baseband signal ends at 2 kHz. Require at least 1 kHz between that edge and \(f_s/2\). Find the lowest rate satisfying this stated margin.
answer:
Sampling rate with a guard margin\[f_s/2-B\ge M\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f_s\ge2(B+M)\]

Substitution / calculation

Write the margin inequality.\[f_s/2-B\ge M\]

Solve for the sampling rate.\[\begin{aligned} f_s\ge2(B+M)&=2(2000+1000)\\[2pt]&=6000\text{ sample/s} \end{aligned}\]

6 ksample/s. Real filter ripple and rejection still need specifications.

question: Only \(x[0]=1\) V and \(x[1]=0.5\) V are nonzero. Using normalized sinc interpolation, find \(y(0)\), \(y(T_s)\) and \(y(T_s/2)\).
answer:
Sinc interpolation\[y(t)=\sum_n x[n]\operatorname{sinc}\bigl((t-nT_s)/T_s\bigr)\]

Substitution / calculation

Add the two shifted contributions.\[y(t)=\operatorname{sinc}(t/T_s)+0.5\operatorname{sinc}(t/T_s-1)\]

At integer positions all nonmatching sinc terms vanish.\[\begin{aligned} y(0)=1\text{ V}\\[2pt]y(T_s)=0.5\text{ V} \end{aligned}\]

At the midpoint use sinc(1/2)=2/pi.\[\begin{aligned} y(T_s/2)&=1.5\frac2\pi\\[2pt]&=0.95493\text{ V} \end{aligned}\]

1 V, 0.5 V and 0.95493 V, respectively. The stated sequence has no other nonzero samples.

question: For \(x(t)=\operatorname{sinc}^2(200t)\) with \(\operatorname{sinc}(u)=\sin(\pi u)/(\pi u)\), find spectral support, baseband bandwidth and Nyquist rate.
answer:
Fourier transform of a sinc pulse\[\operatorname{sinc}(at)\longleftrightarrow\frac1{|a|}\operatorname{rect}(f/a)\]

Substitution / calculation

The transform of sinc(200t) is rectangular on [-100,100] Hz.

Squaring in time convolves the two rectangles in frequency.

Add the support endpoints.\[[-100,100]+[-100,100]=[-200,200]\text{ Hz}\]

Read the positive edge and double it.\[\begin{aligned} B=200\text{ Hz}\\[2pt]R_N&=2(200)\\[2pt]&=400\text{ sample/s} \end{aligned}\]

Triangular spectrum on \([-200,200]\) Hz; bandwidth 200 Hz; Nyquist rate 400 sample/s.

question: Why is sampling exactly at twice a sinusoid frequency not a safe general practical design? Give a phase-dependent example.
answer:
For \(x(t)=\sin(2\pi ft)\) and \(f_s=2f\), samples are \(\sin(\pi n)=0\). The unknown sinusoid amplitude is lost in this sequence. Boundary spectral conditions matter; practical designs use a rate above twice the band limit.

question: Sketch PAM, PWM and PPM pulses for three increasing positive message samples.

PAM pulses become taller. PWM pulses become wider. In the stated positive-sensitivity PPM mapping, pulses move later in their slots. PPM pulse height and width stay fixed.

The dotted vertical lines mark slot boundaries. Pulse height carries PAM information; the distance between edges carries PWM information; displacement from the slot reference carries PPM information.

question: Explain the difference between natural PAM and flat-top PAM.
answer: In natural PAM, the top of each open pulse follows the changing input. In flat-top PAM, the sampled value is held constant for the pulse duration.

question: List two timing requirements for a practical PPM system.
answer:
• A reference or synchronized clock must identify each time slot.

  • The pulse must fit inside its slot, with sufficient separation from neighbouring pulses.

question: Why can a limiter reduce amplitude noise in PWM or PPM?
answer: The message is carried mainly by pulse timing, so unwanted height changes can be clipped. A limiter does not remove timing jitter; noisy edges can still shift the measured width or position.

question: Using the sketch in Question 2.02, which waveform has fixed pulse width and changing pulse position? Explain how to recover the message.
answer: It is PPM. Measure the pulse displacement from the slot reference. Subtract the fixed offset and divide by the position sensitivity. Larger positive displacement represents a larger input for the mapping shown.

question: A message ends at 3.4 kHz. Test an 8 ksample/s sampler. Also find the alias of an unwanted 7 kHz cosine.
answer:
Nyquist rate and aliased frequency\[\begin{aligned} R_N=2B\\[2pt]M=f_s/2-B\\[2pt]f_a=|f-kf_s| \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Compare with the message Nyquist rate.\[\begin{aligned} R_N&=2(3.4)\\[2pt]&=6.8\text{ ksample/s}<8 \end{aligned}\]

Find half-rate margin.\[\begin{aligned} f_s/2-B&=4-3.4\\[2pt]&=0.6\text{ kHz} \end{aligned}\]

Fold the unwanted tone.\[\begin{aligned} f_a&=|7-8|\\[2pt]&=1\text{ kHz} \end{aligned}\]

The rate is above the message boundary, but the 7 kHz interferer aliases to 1 kHz unless removed beforehand.

question: For unit-height rectangular gates centred at \(nT_s\), derive \(c_k\). Evaluate \(c_0\) and \(c_1\) for \(d=0.25\).
answer:
Fourier-series coefficients of a rectangular gate\[c_k=\frac1{T_s}\int_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}e^{-j2\pi kt/T_s}\,dt\]

Substitution / calculation

Integrate one centred gate.\[c_k=\frac1{T_s}\int_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}e^{-j2\pi kt/T_s}dt\]

Use normalized sinc.\[\begin{aligned} c_k=d\operatorname{sinc}(kd)\\[2pt]c_0=d \end{aligned}\]

Substitute the given duty factor.\[\begin{aligned} c_1&=0.25\frac{\sin(0.25\pi)}{0.25\pi}\\[2pt]&=0.22508 \end{aligned}\]

\(c_0=0.25\) and \(c_1=0.22508\); shifting the gate changes coefficient phase.

question: Flat-top samples \(x[0]=1\), \(x[1]=0.5\) and \(x[2]=-0.5\) V are spaced by \(T_s=1\) ms. Each rectangular hold lasts \(\tau=0.4\) ms. Write the output and state the values at 0.2, 0.6 and 1.2 ms.
answer:
Flat-top PAM reconstruction\[\begin{aligned} y(t)=\sum_n x[n]h(t-nT_s)\\[2pt]h(t)=u(t)-u(t-\tau) \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Define a unit hold pulse.\[h(t)=u(t)-u(t-\tau)\]

Shift and scale one pulse for each sample.\[y(t)=h(t)+0.5h(t-T_s)-0.5h(t-2T_s)\]

Check whether each time lies inside a hold interval.\[\begin{aligned} y(0.2\text{ ms})=1\\[2pt]y(0.6\text{ ms})=0\\[2pt]y(1.2\text{ ms})=0.5\text{ V} \end{aligned}\]

The gap at 0.6 ms is zero because the hold lasts less than the sample interval.

question: A hold lasts 50 microseconds. Find its amplitude ratio relative to DC at 4 kHz, attenuation in dB and equalizer gain at that frequency.
answer:
Aperture response and equalization\[\begin{aligned} A(f)=|\operatorname{sinc}(f\tau)|\\[2pt]A_{\rm dB}=20\log_{10}A\\[2pt]G_{\rm eq}=1/A \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Form the dimensionless product.\[\begin{aligned} f\tau&=4000(50\times10^{-6})\\[2pt]&=0.2 \end{aligned}\]

Evaluate the normalized response.\[\begin{aligned} A&=|\operatorname{sinc}(0.2)|\\[2pt]&=0.93549 \end{aligned}\]

Convert the ratio and invert it.\[\begin{aligned} 20\log_{10}A&=20\log_{10}(0.93549)\\[2pt]&=-0.579\text{ dB}\\[2pt]G_{\rm eq}&=1/A\\[2pt]&=1/0.93549\\[2pt]&=1.06896 \end{aligned}\]

0.93549 amplitude ratio; 0.579 dB loss; equalizer gain 1.06896.

question: For \(x(t)=\cos(2\pi1000t)\) V, estimate the largest first-order sample error caused by a timing error of magnitude 1 microsecond.
answer:
First-order timing-jitter error\[\begin{aligned} e_t\simeq x\prime(t)\delta t\\[2pt]\max|x\prime(t)|=2\pi fA \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Use a first-order time expansion.\[e_t\simeq x\prime(t)\delta t\]

The largest sinusoidal slope is 2 pi f A.\[\begin{aligned} \max|x\prime(t)|&=2\pi(1000)(1)\\[2pt]&=6283.19\text{ V/s} \end{aligned}\]

Multiply slope by timing error.\[|e_t|_{\max}\simeq6283.19(10^{-6})=0.006283\text{ V}\]

Approximately 6.283 mV; the small-jitter approximation is used.

question: At 20 ksample/s, a gate lasts 5 microseconds. Find its duty factor and natural-PAM recovery gain.
answer:
Duty factor and recovery gain\[\begin{aligned} T_s=1/f_s\\[2pt]d=\tau/T_s\\[2pt]G=1/d \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Find the slot period.\[\begin{aligned} T_s&=1/20000\\[2pt]&=50\,\mu\text{s} \end{aligned}\]

Divide durations in the same units.\[\begin{aligned} d&=5/50\\[2pt]&=0.1 \end{aligned}\]

Undo the DC scaling.\[\begin{aligned} G&=1/d\\[2pt]&=1/0.1\\[2pt]&=10 \end{aligned}\]

Duty factor 0.1 and gain 10.

question: For \(x(t)=\operatorname{sinc}^2(1000t)\), using normalized sinc, find the positive spectral edge and a practical sampling rate above the boundary.
answer:
Sinc spectrum and Nyquist rate\[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{sinc}(at)\longleftrightarrow\frac1{|a|}\operatorname{rect}(f/a)\\[2pt]R_N=2B \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

The unsquared sinc has support [-500,500] Hz. Convolving that support with itself gives [-1000,1000] Hz.

Calculate the boundary and choose a larger rate.\[\begin{aligned} B=1000\text{ Hz}\\[2pt]R_N&=2(1000)\\[2pt]&=2000\text{ sample/s}\\[2pt]f_s=2500\text{ sample/s} \end{aligned}\]

Positive edge 1 kHz; 2.5 ksample/s is a candidate with margin, subject to filter design.

question: A PWM system uses \(w=8+12x\) microseconds, where \(x\) is in volts. Recover the message from a measured width of 17 microseconds.
answer:
Inverse PWM amplitude relation\[x=(w-w_0)/K_w\]

Substitution / calculation

Remove the baseline width.\[\begin{aligned} w-w_0&=17-8\\[2pt]&=9\,\mu\text{s} \end{aligned}\]

Divide by width sensitivity.\[\begin{aligned} x&=\frac{9\,\mu\text{s}}{12\,\mu\text{s/V}}\\[2pt]&=0.75\text{ V} \end{aligned}\]

The recovered sample is 0.75 V.

question: A ramp rises from 0 to 2 V over 40 microseconds. The output is high while the ramp is below a held 1.2 V sample. Find the pulse width and check the inverse recovery.
answer:
Ramp-comparator PWM relation\[\begin{aligned} w=T_s\frac m{A_r}\\[2pt]m=A_r\frac w{T_s} \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Use equal fractions of ramp amplitude and time.\[\begin{aligned} w&=T_s\frac{m}{A_r}\\[2pt]&=40\frac{1.2}{2}\\[2pt]&=24\,\mu\text{s} \end{aligned}\]

Reverse the mapping.\[\begin{aligned} m&=A_r\frac w{T_s}\\[2pt]&=2\frac{24}{40}\\[2pt]&=1.2\text{ V} \end{aligned}\]

Width 24 microseconds; recovered amplitude 1.2 V.

question: State what remains fixed in trailing-edge PWM and explain how another alignment convention changes the drawing.
answer:
In trailing-edge PWM, the leading edge is fixed and the trailing edge moves. Leading-edge PWM fixes the trailing edge; centre-aligned PWM moves both edges around a fixed centre. The width still represents the message.

question: A PPM pulse begins 18 microseconds after the slot reference. With \(t_0=10\,\mu\)s and \(K_t=20\,\mu\)s/V, find the message voltage.
answer:
Inverse PPM amplitude relation\[x=(t_{\rm start}-t_0)/K_t\]

Substitution / calculation

Remove the offset.\[\begin{aligned} \Delta t&=18-10\\[2pt]&=8\,\mu\text{s} \end{aligned}\]

Divide by the position sensitivity.\[\begin{aligned} x&=8/20\\[2pt]&=0.4\text{ V} \end{aligned}\]

0.4 V.

question: Explain how a moving PWM edge can generate a constant-width PPM pulse. Why must the resulting pulse be checked against the slot end?
answer:
An edge detector triggers a one-shot of fixed duration at the moving PWM edge. The trigger time carries the message. The new pulse may end later than the original edge, so its full width must fit within the allowed timing interval.

question: A rising edge changes by 1 V in 0.2 microseconds. Voltage-noise standard deviation is 20 mV. Estimate timing-error standard deviation.
answer:
Edge slope and timing uncertainty\[\begin{aligned} S_e=\Delta v/\Delta t\\[2pt]\sigma_t\simeq\sigma_v/|S_e| \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Calculate the local slope.\[\begin{aligned} S_e&=1/(0.2\times10^{-6})\\[2pt]&=5\times10^6\text{ V/s} \end{aligned}\]

Convert millivolts and divide by slope magnitude.\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_t\simeq\frac{\sigma_v}{|S_e|}&=\frac{0.020}{5\times10^6}\\[2pt]&=4\text{ ns} \end{aligned}\]

Approximately 4 ns under the small-noise, locally linear-edge approximation.

question: Independent pulse-arrival and reference-clock errors have standard deviations 4 ns and 3 ns. With \(K_t=100\) ns/V, find input-referred uncertainty.
answer:
Independent PPM timing-error propagation\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\Delta t}=\sqrt{\sigma_{\rm arrival}^2+\sigma_{\rm ref}^2}\\[2pt]\sigma_x=\sigma_{\Delta t}/|K_t| \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Combine the independent errors in the measured time difference.\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\Delta t}&=\sqrt{4^2+3^2}\\[2pt]&=5\text{ ns} \end{aligned}\]

Convert timing uncertainty to voltage.\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_x&=\sigma_{\Delta t}/|K_t|\\[2pt]&=5/100\\[2pt]&=0.05\text{ V} \end{aligned}\]

50 mV; a noiseless reference would give 40 mV.

question: Describe the recovery operation for each of PAM, PWM and PPM. Can an amplitude limiter remove all noise?
answer:
PAM measures amplitude and compensates known gain and hold effects. PWM measures width and applies its inverse map. PPM measures clock-relative arrival and applies its inverse map. Filter the recovered sequence to obtain the message. A limiter can suppress amplitude fluctuations in timing schemes, but not all edge jitter; in PAM it also destroys the amplitude information.

question: Derive the quantization-noise power for uniform error on \([-\Delta/2,\Delta/2]\). Then derive the full-scale sinusoidal SQNR for an n-bit uniform quantizer.
answer:
Mean-square quantization noise and SQNR\[\begin{aligned} P_q=\int e^2p_e(e)\,de\\[2pt]\mathrm{SQNR}=P_s/P_q \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Average squared error using the uniform density.\[\begin{aligned} P_q&=\frac1\Delta\int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2}e^2de\\[2pt]&=\frac{\Delta^2}{12} \end{aligned}\]

A full-scale sinusoid of peak A has mean square A squared over two.\[\begin{aligned} P_s=A^2/2\\[2pt]\Delta=2A/2^n \end{aligned}\]

Divide signal power by quantization-noise power.\[\begin{aligned} \frac{P_s}{P_q}&=\frac{A^2/2}{\Delta^2/12}\\[2pt]&=\frac32\,2^{2n} \end{aligned}\]

Convert the ratio to decibels.\[\mathrm{SQNR}_{\rm dB}=10\log_{10}(3/2)+20n\log_{10}2\simeq1.76+6.02n\]

The formula requires a full-scale sinusoid, no overload and the uniform-error model.

question: For normalized input \(x=0.1\) and \(\mu=255\), calculate the mu-law compressor output. Apply the inverse without quantization and explain what changes when quantization is included.
answer:
Mu-law compression\[y=\operatorname{sgn}(x)\frac{\ln(1+\mu|x|)}{\ln(1+\mu)}\]

Substitution / calculation

Use the positive-input compressor law.\[\begin{aligned} y&=\frac{\ln(1+\mu x)}{\ln(1+\mu)}\\[2pt]&=\frac{\ln(1+255(0.1))}{\ln(1+255)}\\[2pt]&=\frac{\ln26.5}{\ln256}\\[2pt]&=0.59099 \end{aligned}\]

Invert the exact unrounded output.\[\begin{aligned} \hat x&=\frac{256^y-1}{255}\\[2pt]&=0.1 \end{aligned}\]

Quantization changes y before expansion. The inverse then expands the quantization error as well as the signal.

\(y\approx0.591\); ideal inverse returns 0.1. Compression alone is reversible, but quantization is not.

question: For normalized input use A-law with \(A=87.6\). Identify which branch applies to \(x=0.005\) and \(x=0.1\), and evaluate the compressed outputs.

Substitution / calculation

The smaller input uses the linear branch.\[\begin{aligned} F(0.005)&=\frac{87.6(0.005)}{1+\ln87.6}\\[2pt]&=0.08003 \end{aligned}\]

The larger input uses the logarithmic branch.\[\begin{aligned} F(0.1)&=\frac{1+\ln(87.6\times0.1)}{1+\ln87.6}\\[2pt]&=0.57927 \end{aligned}\]

Outputs approximately 0.08003 and 0.57927. The compressor is odd for negative inputs.

question: Use DM step \(\Delta=0.2\) V, initial estimate zero, and an upward step when input equals or exceeds the previous estimate. Encode samples \((0.1,0.4,0.3,0)\) V. Give every staircase value.

Compare 0 with 0.2.\[\begin{aligned} b_3=0\\[2pt]\tilde x_3&=0.2-0.2\\[2pt]&=0 \end{aligned}\]

question: An illustrative ADM rule starts at \(\Delta_0=0.1\) V with previous bit 0. After repeated consecutive bits, double the next step, capped at 0.4 V. After a change, halve it, floored at 0.05 V. For bits 1,1,1,0, give the step used for each bit and the next step.

Substitution / calculation

The first bit differs from the reference bit.\[\begin{aligned} \Delta_0=0.1\\[2pt]\Delta_1&=\max(0.1/2,0.05)\\[2pt]&=0.05 \end{aligned}\]

The second bit repeats.\[\begin{aligned} \Delta_2&=\min(2(0.05),0.4)\\[2pt]&=0.1 \end{aligned}\]

The third bit also repeats.\[\begin{aligned} \Delta_3&=\min(2(0.1),0.4)\\[2pt]&=0.2 \end{aligned}\]

The fourth bit changes.\[\begin{aligned} \Delta_4&=\max(0.2/2,0.05)\\[2pt]&=0.1 \end{aligned}\]

Used steps: 0.10,0.05,0.10,0.20 V; next step 0.10 V. The update timing is part of the specified rule.

question: Use predictor \(\hat x[k]=\tilde x[k-1]\), initial reconstructed value zero, and nearest-multiple-of-0.25-V quantization of the prediction error, with no clipping. For input \((0.30,0.70,0.60)\) V, calculate prediction errors, quantized errors and reconstructed samples.

Closed-loop DPCM relations\[\begin{aligned} e[k]=x[k]-\tilde x[k-1]\\[2pt]e_q[k]=Q(e[k])\\[2pt]\tilde x[k]=\tilde x[k-1]+e_q[k] \end{aligned}\]

Process the first sample from the zero state.\[\begin{aligned} e[0]&=0.30-0\\[2pt]&=0.30\\[2pt]e_q[0]=0.25\\[2pt]\tilde x[0]&=0+0.25\\[2pt]&=0.25 \end{aligned}\]

Predict from the reconstructed value, not the original input.\[\begin{aligned} e[1]&=0.70-0.25\\[2pt]&=0.45\\[2pt]e_q[1]=0.50\\[2pt]\tilde x[1]&=0.25+0.50\\[2pt]&=0.75 \end{aligned}\]

question: A DM system samples at five times the Nyquist rate of a 3 kHz message band. The step is 250 mV. Derive and calculate the largest amplitude of a 2 kHz sinusoid that satisfies the slope-tracking condition.

Substitution / calculation

Require staircase slope at least the peak input slope.\[\Delta f_s\ge2\pi f_m A_m\]

question: Four channels each supply 8-bit samples at 8 ksample/s. A frame carries one sample per channel and one framing bit. Find frame size, link rate, frame period, bit interval, payload efficiency and ideal baseband minimum bandwidth.

question: Five telephone channels each have bandwidth 4 kHz and one music channel has bandwidth 20 kHz. Sample each at its theoretical Nyquist rate. Find total PAM sample rate, a possible frame allocation at 8 kframe/s, and the ideal real baseband Nyquist bandwidth. Ignore guard times.

Find individual sample rates.\[\begin{aligned} f_{s,v}=8\text{ ksample/s}\\[2pt]f_{s,m}=40\text{ ksample/s} \end{aligned}\]

Use ideal real PAM Nyquist symbol bandwidth.\[\begin{aligned} B_{\min}&=R_{sample}/2\\[2pt]&=80/2\\[2pt]&=40\text{ kHz} \end{aligned}\]

question: A PCM frame contains 24 channels, each with one 8-bit sample, plus one framing bit. The frame rate is 8000 frame/s. Find payload rate, total rate and the fraction of transmitted bits used for framing.

Substitution / calculation

Count the two parts of a frame.\[\begin{aligned} N_{payload}&=24(8)\\[2pt]&=192\\[2pt]N_f&=192+1\\[2pt]&=193 \end{aligned}\]

Multiply each by frame rate.\[\begin{aligned} R_{payload}&=192(8000)\\[2pt]&=1.536\text{ Mbit/s}\\[2pt]R_{total}&=193(8000)\\[2pt]&=1.544\text{ Mbit/s} \end{aligned}\]

Use total bits in the denominator.\[\begin{aligned} \eta_{\rm framing}&=1/193\times100\%\\[2pt]&=0.5181\% \end{aligned}\]

question: Derive coherent BPSK BER for equal priors, points \(\pm\sqrt{E_b}\) and projected noise variance \(N_0/2\). Evaluate it at \(E_b/N_0=6\) dB. Use \(Q(2.8217)\approx0.002388\).
answer:
BPSK error event and Gaussian tail\[\begin{aligned} P_b=P\{n<-\sqrt{E_b}\}\\[2pt]n\sim\mathcal N(0,N_0/2) \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

With the positive point sent, an error crosses zero.\[P_b=P\{n<-\sqrt{E_b}\}\]

Normalize by the noise standard deviation.\[\begin{aligned} P_b&=Q\left(\frac{\sqrt{E_b}}{\sqrt{N_0/2}}\right)\\[2pt]&=Q(\sqrt{2\gamma_b}) \end{aligned}\]

Convert the given dB ratio.\[\begin{aligned} \gamma_b&=10^{0.6}\\[2pt]&=3.98107 \end{aligned}\]

Evaluate the argument and tail.\[\begin{aligned} \sqrt{2\gamma_b}&=\sqrt{2(3.98107)}\\[2pt]&=2.8217\\[2pt]P_b\approx0.002388 \end{aligned}\]

BER approximately \(2.388\times10^{-3}\) under the stated ideal assumptions.

question: For equiprobable square 16-QAM in ideal coherent AWGN at \(E_b/N_0=10\) dB, calculate symbol-error probability and a high-SNR Gray-coded BER approximation. Use \(Q(\sqrt8)=0.0023389\).
answer:
Square-QAM energy ratio and Gaussian tail\[\begin{aligned} \gamma_s=(\log_2M)\gamma_b\\[2pt]a=Q\!\left(\sqrt{3\gamma_s/(M-1)}\right) \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Convert to linear symbol-energy ratio.\[\begin{aligned} \gamma_b=10\\[2pt]\gamma_s&=4\gamma_b\\[2pt]&=4(10)\\[2pt]&=40 \end{aligned}\]

Form the Q-function argument.\[\begin{aligned} a&=Q\left(\sqrt{\frac{3\gamma_s}{M-1}}\right)\\[2pt]&=Q\left(\sqrt{\frac{3(40)}{16-1}}\right)\\[2pt]&=Q(\sqrt{2(4)})\\[2pt]&=Q(\sqrt8)\\[2pt]&=0.0023389 \end{aligned}\]

Use the square-QAM symbol-error formula.\[\begin{aligned} P_s&=4(1-1/4)a-4(1-1/4)^2a^2\\[2pt]&=3a-2.25a^2 \end{aligned}\]

Calculate the symbol probability and divide approximately by four.\[\begin{aligned} P_s=3(0.0023389)-2.25(0.0023389)^2\approx0.0070043\\[2pt]P_b\approx P_s/4&=0.0070043/4\\[2pt]&=0.0017511 \end{aligned}\]

SER about 0.0070043; Gray BER about 0.0017511. The BER relation is an approximation, not an exact identity.

question: Estimate the high-SNR SER and Gray BER of coherent 8-PSK at \(E_b/N_0=12\) dB. Use \(Q(3.7318)\approx9.507\times10^{-5}\). State the approximation involved.
answer:
Nearest-neighbour M-PSK error approximation\[\begin{aligned} \gamma_s=(\log_2M)\gamma_b\\[2pt]P_s\simeq2Q\!\left(\sqrt{2\gamma_s}\sin(\pi/M)\right) \end{aligned}\]

Substitution / calculation

Convert bit ratio to symbol ratio.\[\begin{aligned} \gamma_b&=10^{1.2}\\[2pt]&=15.8489\\[2pt]\gamma_s&=3\gamma_b\\[2pt]&=3(15.8489)\\[2pt]&=47.5468 \end{aligned}\]

Use the nearest-neighbour PSK approximation.\[P_s\simeq2Q\left(\sqrt{2\gamma_s}\sin(\pi/8)\right)\]

Calculate the distance argument.\[\sqrt{2(47.5468)}\sin(\pi/8)\simeq3.7318\]

Divide approximately by the three bits per symbol.\[\begin{aligned} P_s\simeq2Q(3.7318)\simeq1.90\times10^{-4}\\[2pt]P_b\simeq(1.90\times10^{-4})/3\simeq6.33\times10^{-5} \end{aligned}\]

Approximate SER \(1.90\times10^{-4}\) and Gray BER \(6.33\times10^{-5}\); nearest-neighbour errors are assumed dominant.
